prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I still prefer B013, and I have narrowed the claim I make for it. What I would ask the committee to recognise is the Kane-Mele prediction of a time-reversal-protected quantum spin Hall phase with a Z2 invariant, and Molenkamp's observation of the helical edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells. This is a prediction-then-observation arc, confirmed over nearly two decades in many independent materials and probes, and its central idea, symmetry-protected band topology, now organises work in photonics, cold atoms and mechanical systems. None of that content was part of the 2016 citation, which concerned topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall and Haldane-chain tradition. I value a result whose conceptual content survives a change of platform, and that is the property that distinguishes this candidate from the others on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The attribution objection raised by Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Kroll and Pearce is serious and I have not resolved it. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal sits directly between Kane-Mele and Molenkamp, and Hasan's three-dimensional work is a separate strand; a three-name cap excludes both. I now think my round-1 treatment of this was too light: for a citation limited to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp to be defensible it has to be explicitly scoped to the two-dimensional prediction and its first observation, and I accept that some colleagues will regard that as an incomplete account of the history. The 2016 overlap is also a real cost in appetite even though I do not think it is a cost in substance. B053 has the cleaner credit and the broadest support, and if the committee decides that attribution cleanliness should decide, B053 is a legitimate prize that I could vote for.

responses.point: Danielsson accepts that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a more defensible core than his opening trio, but says B013 carries an allocation problem about as hard as the Higgs one (Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, the 2D versus 3D split) without the compensating centrality.
responses.response: I thank him for the concession on Mele, and I agree the allocation problem is real. But I do not think it is as hard as the Higgs one: the Higgs choice among four named figures in two collaborations of thousands is a choice among near-equivalent leadership roles, whereas here the 2D claim can be bounded by the physics, namely the prediction of the Z2 spin Hall phase and the first observation of its edge transport. The 3D strand then falls outside the citation by construction, not by arbitrary exclusion. On centrality I accept his point that the Higgs is at the centre of fundamental physics, and I would not dispute that the discovery deserves recognition. My worry is exactly the one he states: a three-from-four allocation of a collaboration-scale result looks arbitrary in a way the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp line does not.

responses.point: Eriksson would give B033 the edge because it is untouched by an earlier prize and has a cleaner three-name credit, but says he could support B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp if the 2016 overlap is addressed directly in the citation.
responses.response: This is the most useful question put to me, and I take it directly. My citation now names the quantum spin Hall effect, the Z2 classification and the HgTe observation, which the 2016 prize did not mention, so the distinction is stated in the text and not left to the reader. On B033 I still hold that the pairing mechanism, device variability and the absence of Yuan Cao from the credited names make it earlier than B013. I do not think the two are rivals, as he says, and I would be content to see B033 prized in a later cycle. I do concede that his credit for B033 is tidier than mine, and that is the strongest argument against my own position.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B013 as his first alternative but would not put it ahead of B053 on cleanliness of attribution, because the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Hasan strands fall outside any three-name set.
responses.response: I agree that cleanliness favours B053, and I do not claim otherwise. Where I differ is that cleanliness of credit is a property of the prize and not a measure of how much the discovery changed physics. His own conflict note also matters here: he spent time in Hall's laboratory, whose frequency-comb work is an enabling tool for lattice clocks, and he is the member who most clearly names the 2005 and 2012 prizes as nearby. I think the overlap with the clock is closer than the overlap I am accused of with 2016, since a lattice clock inherits the comb and ion-control technology it depends on. He and Lindroth answer that magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms is separable, and I accept that argument, but then the same standard should be applied to the quantum spin Hall prediction relative to 2016.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, says the three-name cap excludes Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and Hasan so that any three-person B013 prize feels structurally unfair, and that he would not resist B013 but would not rank it above B053.
responses.response: I take the fairness point seriously, and I think it is the right test. The difficulty is that every candidate with a three-name cap on this shortlist excludes someone: B053 leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow, B033 leaves out Yuan Cao, B052 leaves out Krivanek, Dellby and Zach, and B046 leaves out two of the four. So the question for the committee is not whether anyone is omitted but whether the omitted contribution is of the same kind as the credited ones. For B013 I would answer that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the decisive HgTe proposal, which I cannot dismiss, but the first demonstration that such an edge state exists belongs to Kane-Mele in theory and to Molenkamp in experiment. I recognise that this is a judgment and I do not insist on it.

responses.point: Lindroth would write the B053 citation around the magic-wavelength lattice scheme, with Katori credited for the proposal and Ye for the accuracy programme and many-body regime, and regards the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I accept that a citation written around the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and neutral-atom statistics would make B053 separable from the frequency-comb and single-ion prizes, and this moves me modestly: I regard B053 as a stronger prize than I did in round 1. I still see a difference in the kind of achievement: a clock is a precision realisation that can be reproduced and compared, whereas B013 introduces a concept that other fields take over. But the statutes honour discovery or invention, and I accept that the lattice clock is a genuine invention. For that reason I keep B053 as my first alternative and would vote for it without reservation if B013 cannot gather support.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a citation for B013 that is deliberately scoped to the two-dimensional prediction and first observation, and so leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and Hasan by construction.
Whether Molenkamp or Hasan should hold the third place alongside Kane and Mele; I hold Molenkamp because the quantum spin Hall observation is the one that closes the prediction-then-observation arc.
How heavily to weight the 2016 prize against B013 when the citation is explicit about what that prize did not recognise, since opinions in the first round remain divided.

Whether four members preferring B053 and the cleaner credit should settle the matter against a conceptually stronger but less cleanly attributed candidate. I have not changed my preferred configuration, but I would not regard B053 as an error.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has arisen since round 1. My documented co-authors and institutions (Gothenburg, Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg) do not include any credited name on the shortlist, and no connection to B013, B053 or B033 is documented in my profile. My work on statistical descriptions of complex systems and neural networks is not part of any shortlisted discovery.
